newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO-led force goes on heightened alert in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: NATO-led force goes on heightened alert in Bosnia.

text.p: The NATO-led peace force in Bosnia went on heightened alert this week due to a security threat reported at a base in the capital Sarajevo, alliance officers and Western officials said on Wednesday.

Soldiers in the multinational Stabilisation Force (SFOR) were ordered on Tuesday not to travel alone and to have a flak jacket, helmet and weapon on hand as a precaution, NATO officers, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
The alert was issued following a "security threat" at an SFOR base on Monday in Rajlovac on the outskirts of Sarajevo, where German and other SFOR troops are stationed.
NATO officers would not specify the nature of the threat. A Bosnian source alleged a truck armed with an explosive was found on Monday at the base but NATO could not confirm the report.
The alliance has been closely monitoring threats against its peacekeeping troops since it launched an arrest operation last month against two Serbs indicted for war crimes.
One suspect was seized and extradited to the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague and another was shot dead after he resisted arrest.

The NATO raid sparked a wave of retaliatory bombings and attacks against international monitors and peacekeeping soldiers. No one was killed in the Serb revenge campaign and the low-level violence has since tapered off.
A survey sponsored by the United States Information Agency has found increased hostility among Serbs towards SFOR since the raid on indicted war criminals.

Some 66 percent of Bosnian Serbs said they opposed the presence of the NATO-led troops, 86 percent said they lacked confidence in the force and 84 percent said SFOR should not actively search for indicted war criminals.

The security threat coincided with an announcement by SFOR that it planned to crack down on unauthorised special police, including units which help guard indicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic.

SFOR began inspecting special police stations across Serb territory this week as part of the tougher policy. Two anti-tank rocket launchers and small arms ammunition were seized on Tuesday in the Banja Luka area and later destroyed, an SFOR spokesman said.

The 2,000 to 3,000-strong special police brigade in Bosnia's Serb entity are armed with tanks, artillery, armoured personnel carriers, automatic rifles and other weapons associated with military forces.
Under United Nations guidelines, police in Bosnia are allowed to have only one rifle per 10 police officers.

U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke, who brokered the peace treaty that ended the 1992-95 Bosnian war, said last week the special police should have been treated as military forces since the beginning of the NATO deployment in 1995.
NATO Supreme Allied Commander General Wesley Clark, who ordered the more agressive approach, travelled to Bosnia on Wednesday to discuss the policy with SFOR officers.
Moving against Bosnian Serb special police has fuelled speculation that Western governments may be preparing for a possible arrest action against Karadzic, indicted twice by the U.N. tribunal.
